payload.body: An equivalent-rectangular-bandwidth (ERB) is a human-made, frequency-dependent unit of filter bandwidth used to describe the frequency selectivity of the auditory periphery. It is defined as the width of a rectangular (flat) bandpass filter that would pass the same energy as a given auditory filter centered at frequency f. The standard empirical expression is ERB(f) = 24.7·(4.37·f + 1), with f in kHz and the result in Hz, so the equivalent width is about 104 Hz near 0.1 kHz and grows toward roughly 100·f at high frequencies — the auditory filter narrows relative to its center as f rises. Parameters: (1) the center frequency f (kHz); (2) the chosen fitting curve — the Glasberg & Moore (1990) expression is canonical, with alternative fits in the literature. Persistence mechanism: it persists as a standard psychophysically derived formula carried in the audiology and auditory-modeling literature (Glasberg & Moore 1990; Moore's auditory-filter and loudness work) and applied operationally to set the spacing and bandwidth of gammatone, bark, and auditory-filter-bank filters. Boundary: it is a unit of measure — a single number in Hz attached to a center frequency — not the auditory filter itself, not a signal's spectral bandwidth, and distinct from the generic signal-processing 'bandwidth' entry. payload.body: Shimmer (amplitude perturbation) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the cycle-to-cycle variation of amplitude in a voiced speech signal. For a voiced segment segmented into N consecutive glottal cycles, each with amplitude A_i (peak or RMS of cycle i), the perturbation is the normalized cycle difference: APQ3 = (1/(3N)) * sum_i |A_{i+1} - A_i| / ( (1/N) * sum_i A_i ), or equivalently the standard deviation of the cycle amplitudes divided by their mean, reported in percent or in dB (20*log10(std/mean)). Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, (2) the per-cycle amplitude measure (peak or RMS), (3) the perturbation variant (APQ3 quotient or standard deviation). Small shimmer indicates amplitude stability (normal phonation); large shimmer indicates amplitude instability (dysphonia). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by acoustic analysis software (Praat, laryngology toolkits) from pitch-synchronous amplitude tracks; it persists as a documented measurement in voice-disorder assessment.
